statement: WebMvcTags.outcome(HttpServletResponse response) keeps its tag dimension finite: for a null response, and for a response whose getStatus() returns any int, the result is a Tag whose key is "outcome" and whose value is one of INFORMATIONAL, SUCCESS, REDIRECTION, CLIENT_ERROR, SERVER_ERROR and UNKNOWN, and nothing is thrown. Shared by the tasks finite-outcome-before and finite-outcome-after: one property and domain, two artifact-bound claim identities. Established says this one tag dimension of this one entry has at most six values; it says nothing about the server, the release, or the other tags.
assert: result != null && result.getKey().equals("outcome") && (result.getValue().equals("INFORMATIONAL") || result.getValue().equals("SUCCESS") || result.getValue().equals("REDIRECTION") || result.getValue().equals("CLIENT_ERROR") || result.getValue().equals("SERVER_ERROR") || result.getValue().equals("UNKNOWN"))

assumptions.text: A non-null response is a carrier whose getStatus() returns one fixed int, with no other effect, and whose other methods are never called; the claim ranges over that int.
assumptions.basis: The same domain as claims/outcome-preservation.json, read from the source at both commits: each revision calls getStatus() once and no other method of the response.

assumptions.text: Class initialization runs as on the JVM, never removed (WebMvcTags's static initializer with its two Pattern.compile calls; before's WebMvcTags$1 and HttpStatus.Series; after's Outcome).
assumptions.basis: The brief's safety rules. An initializer the checker can't run is a refusal, not an assumption.

assumptions.text: unwind 16 leaves the domain unbounded: before's only loop is five iterations over HttpStatus.Series.values(); after has none.
assumptions.basis: Read from the source at both commits and at Spring Framework v5.2.0.RC2.

notes: No throws clause: an exception is observed, so a revision that throws fails the property rather than escaping it.
The assert names the six values literally; it is the seed's statement (finite-outcome-domain), not the patch's enum, so a seventh value on either side refutes it.

The 200-boundary mutant (controls/status-200.patch) still gives one of the six values, so it satisfies this property by design: this property bounds the label set and can't see a misclassification. The mutant's failing contract is the preservation claim and the oracle's range statement. A stronger range property, value as a function of status, would need the status in the assert, which the response parameter hides; it is not claimed here.
